getDesignGroupSequential.label: O'Brien-Fleming-type alpha spending, 3 looks
getDesignGroupSequential.description: The most common group sequential design in practice: three analyses (two interim, one final) with an O'Brien-Fleming-type alpha spending function, one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%.
getDesignGroupSequential.interpretation: Look at the efficacy boundaries on the z-value scale: the first interim boundary (about 3.71) is far stricter than the fixed-design 1.96, so an early stop needs overwhelming evidence. The final boundary (about 1.99) is barely above 1.96 - the price paid for two interim looks is small. Check the inflation factor: the maximum sample size grows by only about 2%. This is why O'Brien-Fleming-type designs dominate confirmatory practice. (Compare with typeOfDesign = "OF", the classic Wang-Tsiatis version: similar shape, boundaries 3.47 / 2.45 / 2.00.)

getDesignGroupSequential.label: Pocock-type alpha spending, 3 looks
getDesignGroupSequential.description: Same trial as the O'Brien-Fleming example but with a Pocock-type spending function, which spends alpha nearly evenly across looks. Run both and compare on the Summary and Plot tabs.
getDesignGroupSequential.interpretation: The boundaries are nearly constant across stages (about 2.28 at every look), so stopping early is much easier than under O'Brien-Fleming - but the final boundary is well above 1.96, and the inflation factor is much larger. Pocock-type designs pay a real sample-size premium for aggressive early stopping, which is why they are less used for confirmatory trials.

getDesignGroupSequential.label: Adding a non-binding futility bound
getDesignGroupSequential.description: A two-stage O'Brien-Fleming-type design with a futility bound at the interim: if the z-value falls below 0 (the treatment looks no better than control), the trial may stop for futility. Non-binding means the efficacy boundaries remain valid even if the futility rule is ignored.
getDesignGroupSequential.interpretation: The summary now shows a futility boundary at the interim alongside the efficacy boundary. Because it is non-binding, the type I error is protected even if the sponsor continues despite crossing it; a binding futility bound would buy slightly lower efficacy boundaries in exchange for the obligation to stop. Note the 'futility probabilities' row: that is the chance of stopping for futility if the true effect is zero.

getDesignInverseNormal.label: Inverse normal combination, unequal information
getDesignInverseNormal.description: A three-stage adaptive design using the inverse normal combination test with O'Brien-Fleming-type spending and interim analyses at 40% and 70% of the information. The boundaries match the group sequential design - the difference is what the design permits later.
getDesignInverseNormal.interpretation: Compare this summary with getDesignGroupSequential using the same inputs: the boundaries are identical. The inverse normal design combines stage-wise p-values with fixed weights (derived from the planned information rates), which is what makes design adaptations - like a data-driven sample size increase at an interim - possible without inflating the type I error. That flexibility is invisible in the boundary table but is the whole point.

getDesignFisher.label: Fisher's combination test, 2 stages
getDesignFisher.description: A two-stage adaptive design based on Fisher's product of stage-wise p-values, with equal alpha for both stages and early stopping for futility if the first-stage p-value exceeds 0.5.
getDesignFisher.interpretation: Fisher's combination multiplies the stage-wise p-values and compares the product against a critical value. The summary shows the scale: critical values here live on the p-value product scale, not the z-scale. alpha0Vec = 0.5 means the trial stops for futility at stage 1 if p1 > 0.5. Fisher designs are fully adaptive but generally less efficient than inverse normal designs, so they appear mostly in small exploratory settings.

getDesignConditionalDunnett.label: Conditional Dunnett, interim at half the information
getDesignConditionalDunnett.description: A design for multi-arm trials with treatment selection: several treatment arms are compared with a shared control at an interim (at 50% of the information), promising arms continue, and the final analysis uses the conditional Dunnett test to protect the familywise error rate.
getDesignConditionalDunnett.interpretation: This design has no boundary table like the group sequential designs - the interim is for selecting arms, not for early efficacy claims. secondStageConditioning = TRUE conditions the final test on the first-stage data, which is more powerful than treating the stages independently. Use this design as input to the multi-arm analysis functions to see it in action.

getDesignCharacteristics.label: Characteristics of a saved design
getDesignCharacteristics.description: Computes the information and power characteristics of a design. It builds on the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design: create it in the Design tab and save it (the Learn path does this for you), then pick it in the design dropdown below.
getDesignCharacteristics.interpretation: The key numbers are the shift values: how much more information (roughly, sample size) the sequential design needs than a fixed design with the same alpha and power. For the O'Brien-Fleming example the inflation factor is about 1.02 - a 2% premium buys two chances to stop early. The average sample number (ASN) rows show the flip side: under the alternative, the expected sample size is well below the fixed-design requirement.

getPowerAndAverageSampleNumber.label: Power curve for a saved design
getPowerAndAverageSampleNumber.description: Computes overall power, stopping probabilities, and expected sample size of a saved design across a range of standardized effect sizes. It uses the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design from your saved work - create and save it in the Design tab if it isn't there yet.
getPowerAndAverageSampleNumber.interpretation: Read the table by column, one column per effect size theta. At theta = 0 the 'power' row shows the type I error (0.025); as theta grows, power rises and the average sample number (ASN) falls below nMax, because large effects make early stopping likely. This trade-off - a small maximum sample size premium for a much smaller expected sample size - is the core argument for group sequential designs. The Plot tab shows the same story as curves.

getGroupSequentialProbabilities.label: Exit probabilities for O'Brien-Fleming boundaries
getGroupSequentialProbabilities.description: The low-level engine behind the design functions: given a decision matrix of continuation regions (here the classic 3-look O'Brien-Fleming z-boundaries with no futility stopping) and the information rates, it computes the stage-wise boundary-crossing probabilities under the null hypothesis.
getGroupSequentialProbabilities.interpretation: Each column is a stage. The rows give the cumulative probabilities of falling below the lower row and above the upper row of the decision matrix under the null (drift 0). Check that the probabilities of crossing the upper boundaries sum (across stages, as increments) to alpha = 0.025 - that is exactly the constraint the design functions solve for when they compute boundaries. This function is worth one run just to demystify where the boundaries come from.

getFutilityBounds.label: Converting a futility bound between scales
getFutilityBounds.description: Futility rules are communicated on many scales - z-values, p-values, conditional power. This converts a futility bound of z = 0.5 to the one-sided p-value scale.
getFutilityBounds.interpretation: A z-value futility bound of 0.5 corresponds to a one-sided p-value of about 0.31: the trial would stop for futility when the interim result is weaker than p = 0.31. Being able to restate a rule on the scale your clinical team thinks in (often conditional power) is a routine communication task - try changing targetScale and see how the same rule reads on each scale.

getAnalysisResults.label: The interim decision: continue or stop?
getAnalysisResults.description: The chapter-1 trial is running under the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design, and two stages are in. This is the analysis a data monitoring committee sees: observed effect, test statistic against the boundary, and what to do next. Uses the 'Interim data (continuous)' dataset from the Enter data tab (the Learn path creates it for you). nPlanned is the stage-3 sample size still to come.
getAnalysisResults.interpretation: Read the stage-2 column like a monitoring committee: the overall test statistic (2.26) has not crossed the efficacy boundary (2.51), so the test action says continue - close is not crossed, that is the discipline the boundaries buy. The forward-looking numbers say continuing is promising: conditional power 90% with the planned 44 remaining subjects, and the repeated confidence interval has narrowed to [-0.06, 1.01], almost excluding zero. Change means2 in the data to see how quickly this picture turns.

getAnalysisResults.label: Interim analysis, binary endpoint
getAnalysisResults.description: The same monitoring-committee analysis for a response-rate trial: two of three stages in, 40 subjects per group per stage, responders 12 then 19 (treatment) versus 6 then 13 (control). Create the dataset on the Enter data tab (pick 'Binary', the form is pre-filled) and select it below.
getAnalysisResults.interpretation: The overall test statistic climbs from 1.61 to 2.05 - closer, but still short of the stage-2 boundary of 2.51, so the action stays 'continue'. The repeated confidence interval for the rate difference, [-0.03, 0.33] after stage 2, still touches zero. Binary endpoints carry less information per subject than continuous ones, and you can see it: similar-looking data, weaker evidence.

getAnalysisResults.label: Interim analysis, survival endpoint
getAnalysisResults.description: Interim monitoring for a time-to-event trial. Survival data enter as cumulative events and log-rank statistics per stage: 38 events (log-rank 1.66) at look 1, 78 events (2.11) at look 2. Create the dataset on the Enter data tab (pick 'Survival') and select it below.
getAnalysisResults.interpretation: The log-rank statistic of 2.11 at stage 2 has not crossed the boundary of 2.51: continue. The repeated confidence interval for the hazard ratio, about [0.91, 2.85], still includes 1. Note what the data entry asked for - cumulative events and log-rank statistics, not subject-level survival times: that stage-wise summary is exactly what a statistician receives from a data manager at an interim.

getStageResults.label: The machinery under the analysis
getStageResults.description: The stage-wise building blocks behind getAnalysisResults: overall effects, test statistics, and p-values per stage. Save the result - the stage-results object is what the final-inference and test-action functions consume.
getStageResults.interpretation: The overall test statistics (1.87 at stage 1, 2.26 at stage 2) are computed from the cumulative data - each stage folds in everything before it. Save this result under the suggested name 'Stage Results' and feed it to 'Test Actions', 'Final P Value', or 'Conditional Rejection Probabilities' in the picker: that chain - data to stage results to inference - is exactly how an rpact analysis script is structured.

getRepeatedConfidenceIntervals.label: Confidence intervals you may quote mid-trial
getRepeatedConfidenceIntervals.description: Naive confidence intervals computed at an interim are too narrow - they ignore the repeated looks. Repeated confidence intervals stay valid at every stage of the group sequential design.
getRepeatedConfidenceIntervals.interpretation: Watch the intervals tighten as data accumulates: [-0.66, 1.78] after stage 1, [-0.06, 1.01] after stage 2. Both are wider than a naive t-interval on the same data - that width is the honest price of looking early, and it is why interim estimates quoted to a monitoring committee should always be repeated CIs, not standard ones.

getObservedInformationRates.label: Are we where the plan said we would be?
getObservedInformationRates.description: The design planned its looks at 33%, 67%, and 100% of the information (here, 132 subjects). This checks the plan against reality: with 88 subjects observed, what information fractions were the looks actually at?
getObservedInformationRates.interpretation: Here recruitment matched the plan exactly (0.333, 0.667), so nothing needs adjusting. In real trials it never does: stages land at unplanned information fractions, and this function feeds the recalculated rates back into the analysis so the alpha spending stays honest. It is the quiet bookkeeping that makes group sequential designs work in practice.

getSimulationMeans.label: Does the design deliver what the formulas promised?
getSimulationMeans.description: Simulate the chapter-1 trial run under the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design: 1000 simulated trials at effect 0 (the null) and at effect 0.5, with the per-stage sample sizes from the sample size calculation. The seed makes the run exactly reproducible.
getSimulationMeans.interpretation: Read the 'overall reject' row against what theory promised: about 1.9% rejection at effect 0 (the 2.5% type I error, within simulation noise) and about 81% at effect 0.5 (the designed 80% power). The expected sample size, about 112, sits right at the analytic 110. This agreement is the point: simulation validates the formulas - and once you trust it, it can answer questions the formulas cannot. Note plannedSubjects is cumulative across stages, and try more iterations to watch the noise shrink.

getSimulationRates.label: Checking the binary-endpoint calculation
getSimulationRates.description: Simulate the chapter-1 rates trial: 325 subjects (the analytic answer for 45% vs 30%), 1000 simulated trials at pi1 = 0.30 (null) and pi1 = 0.45.
getSimulationRates.interpretation: About 2.9% rejection under the null and 79% at pi1 = 0.45 - the analytic 80% recovered by brute force. For a fixed design this is a round trip; the payoff comes when you perturb assumptions the formula bakes in: try pi2 = 0.35 (a sicker control group than planned) and watch what happens to power without changing the sample size.

getSimulationSurvival.label: A survival trial in silico
getSimulationSurvival.description: Simulate the chapter-3 survival trial: 247 planned events, 429 subjects accrued over 12 months, control median 12 months, at hazard ratios 0.7 and 1.0. Benefit is a hazard ratio below 1, hence directionUpper = FALSE.
getSimulationSurvival.interpretation: About 79% power at hazard ratio 0.7 and 2.1% at 1.0, matching the analytic design. The extra insight only simulation gives: the analysis-time row shows trials under the alternative finish around month 21 rather than month 24, because an effective treatment... slows event accumulation but the trial stops at 247 events whenever they arrive. Simulation turns a sample size table into a calendar you can plan against.

getSimulationMultiArmMeans.label: Pick the best of three arms at an interim
getSimulationMultiArmMeans.description: Three active treatment arms against a shared control, with the best-performing arm selected at the interim and carried to stage 2. Needs a 2-stage inverse normal design: create one in the Design tab (Design Inverse Normal, kMax = 2) and save it, then it appears in the design dropdown.
getSimulationMultiArmMeans.interpretation: The 'reject at least one' row is the familywise power: about 2.7% when no arm works (the protected familywise error) and about 66% when the best arm has effect 0.5. The selected-arms table shows how often each arm survives the interim. There is no closed-form sample size formula for this design - selection rules, multiplicity, and staging interact - which is exactly why multi-arm trials are designed by simulation.

getSimulationEnrichmentMeans.label: Enrich for the subgroup that benefits
getSimulationEnrichmentMeans.description: A population-enrichment trial: a biomarker-positive subgroup ('S', 40% of patients, effect 0.5) and the rest ('R', effect 0.1). At the interim the design can restrict enrollment to the subpopulation where the treatment works. Uses the same saved 2-stage inverse normal design as the multi-arm example.

args.effectList: list(subGroups = c("S", "R"), prevalences = c(0.4, 0.6), stDevs = 1, effects = matrix(c(0.5, 0.1), nrow = 1))

getSimulationEnrichmentMeans.interpretation: About 83% probability of rejecting at least one hypothesis, even though the full-population effect is diluted (0.4 x 0.5 + 0.6 x 0.1 = 0.26) - the interim enrichment rescues power by focusing stage 2 where the effect lives. This design family is the statistical backbone of biomarker-driven oncology trials, and like multi-arm designs it has no formula: simulation is the design tool.

getSampleSizeMeans.label: Continuous endpoint, fixed design
getSampleSizeMeans.description: The textbook calculation: a two-sample comparison of means with standardized effect 0.5 (difference 0.5, standard deviation 1), one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%, no interim analyses.
getSampleSizeMeans.interpretation: About 128 subjects in total (64 per group) - the classic answer for a medium standardized effect. Two things worth internalizing: sample size scales with (stDev/alternative)^2, so halving the effect quadruples the trial; and the efficacy boundary on the treatment-effect scale (0.35) tells you the smallest observed difference that would reach significance.

getSampleSizeMeans.label: Same trial with a group sequential design
getSampleSizeMeans.description: The identical means comparison, but run under the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design from the Design tab. The design dropdown below picks it from your saved work (the Learn path saves it for you if you haven't).
getSampleSizeMeans.interpretation: Compare with the fixed-design example: the maximum sample size rises only from about 128 to 129 (the 2% inflation factor at work), but the expected sample size under the alternative drops to about 110, because the trial can stop at 43 or 86 subjects if the effect shows early. This pair of numbers - small maximum premium, large expected saving - is the entire sales pitch for group sequential designs.

getSampleSizeRates.label: Binary endpoint, 45% vs 30% response
getSampleSizeRates.description: A two-sample comparison of response rates: treatment is assumed to lift the response rate from 30% to 45%, one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%, normal approximation.
getSampleSizeRates.interpretation: About 325 subjects in total for a 15-percentage-point improvement. Note how much larger this is than the continuous-endpoint example: binary endpoints carry less information per subject. Try moving pi2 to 0.5 while keeping the same 15-point difference - the required sample size grows, because variance pi(1-pi) is maximal near 0.5.

getSampleSizeSurvival.label: Survival endpoint, HR 0.7, median control survival 12 months
getSampleSizeSurvival.description: A time-to-event trial: control median survival 12 months, target hazard ratio 0.7, subjects accrued uniformly over 12 months with 12 months of additional follow-up, one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%.
getSampleSizeSurvival.interpretation: The driver of a survival trial is events, not subjects: about 247 events are needed for HR 0.7, and with this accrual and follow-up that translates into about 429 subjects and a 24-month trial. Play with followUpTime and watch the trade: longer follow-up means fewer subjects (each contributes more events) but a longer study - a budget-versus-calendar decision every survival trial faces.

getSampleSizeSurvival.label: Piecewise accrual and piecewise hazards
getSampleSizeSurvival.description: A more realistic setup: sites ramp up (15 subjects/month for the first year, 30/month for the second), and the control hazard is piecewise - 0.025/month in months 0-6, 0.04 in months 6-12, 0.015 thereafter. Target hazard ratio 0.7.
getSampleSizeSurvival.interpretation: The event requirement (about 247) is the same as in the simple example - it depends only on the hazard ratio, alpha, and power. What changes is everything else: 540 subjects accrue over 24 months, and because the late hazard is low (0.015/month), events arrive slowly - the required follow-up is about 25 months and the analysis lands near month 49. This is why realistic accrual and hazard assumptions matter: the statistics are the same, the calendar is not.

getSampleSizeCounts.label: Recurrent events, negative binomial
getSampleSizeCounts.description: A count-data endpoint (e.g. exacerbations per year): control rate 0.8 events per subject-year, target rate ratio 0.75, overdispersion 0.5, everyone observed for exactly one year.
getSampleSizeCounts.interpretation: About 744 subjects - count endpoints with overdispersion are expensive. Set overdispersion to 0 and rerun: the requirement drops sharply, because overdispersion (patient-to-patient heterogeneity beyond Poisson) dilutes the information each subject contributes. Under-guessing this parameter at the design stage is one of the classic ways recurrent-event trials end up underpowered.

getPowerMeans.label: Power curve under a saved sequential design
getPowerMeans.description: The flip side of sample size: fix the maximum sample size at 128 and ask what power the saved 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design achieves across a range of standardized effects. If it isn't in your saved work yet, create and save it in the Design tab first.
getPowerMeans.interpretation: Read the cumulative power row: 20% at effect 0.2, 61% at 0.4, 92% at 0.6, 99% at 0.8 - the S-shaped power curve every trialist carries in their head. Also read the expected-sample-size rows: at effect 0.8 the trial stops early so often that it averages just 85 subjects of the 128 maximum. The Plot tab draws both curves.

getPowerRates.label: Power for a range of response rates, n = 200
getPowerRates.description: With 200 subjects and a control response rate of 30%, how much power is there to detect treatment response rates from 40% to 60%?
getPowerRates.interpretation: Power climbs from 32% (pi1 = 0.40) through 59% (0.45) and 83% (0.50) to 99% (0.60). The sobering lesson: with n = 200, a real 10-point improvement is more likely missed than found. Power calculations before a trial protect you from exactly this - running a study that cannot answer its own question.

getPowerSurvival.label: Power for a range of hazard ratios, 200 events
getPowerSurvival.description: A survival trial with 400 subjects and 200 target events (control median 12 months, 12-month accrual): what is the power if the true hazard ratio is 0.6, 0.7, or 0.8?
getPowerSurvival.interpretation: Power is 95% at HR 0.6, 71% at 0.7, and only 35% at 0.8 - survival trials sized for optimistic hazard ratios are fragile against moderate effects. Note directionUpper = FALSE: benefit means a hazard ratio below 1, so power is directed towards smaller values; forgetting this flag computes power for the wrong tail (run it with TRUE and see the powers collapse).

getPowerCounts.label: Power for recurrent events, n = 400
getPowerCounts.description: With 400 subjects, control rate 0.8 events/year, and overdispersion 0.5: what is the power to detect rate ratios of 0.7 or 0.8? Benefit is a ratio below 1, hence directionUpper = FALSE.
getPowerCounts.interpretation: Power is about 71% for a rate ratio of 0.7 but only 37% for 0.8 - halving the effect (on the log scale) costs roughly half the power here. Together with the sample-size example (744 subjects for 80% power at ratio 0.75), this brackets the realistic operating range for the design.

getEventProbabilities.label: How fast do events accumulate?
getEventProbabilities.description: For a trial with 400 subjects accrued over 12 months, control hazard 0.05/month, and hazard ratio 0.8: what fraction of subjects will have had an event at months 6 through 30?
getEventProbabilities.interpretation: The cumulative event probability grows from 6% at month 6 to 23% at month 12 and 65% at month 30 - multiply by 400 to translate into expected event counts. This is the tool for answering the planning question survival designs live and die by: when will we reach the target number of events? Note the treatment arm (probabilities '1') lags the control arm - effective treatment slows down your own trial.

getNumberOfSubjects.label: Recruitment curve with a ramp-up
getNumberOfSubjects.description: Sites recruit 15 subjects/month for the first 6 months and 30/month for the next 6. How many subjects are on study at months 3 through 24?
getNumberOfSubjects.interpretation: The curve runs 45, 90, 180, 270 and then flattens - accrual ends at month 12 with 270 subjects (6 x 15 + 6 x 30). Piecewise accrual notation reads as intervals: c(0, 6, 12) with intensities c(15, 30) means 15/month on [0, 6) and 30/month on [6, 12]. Getting this notation right here makes the survival sample size functions, which use the same convention, much easier to read.

getAccrualTime.label: From relative site capacity to absolute intensities
getAccrualTime.description: Planned recruitment is known in relative terms - the second period runs at 1.5x the rate of the first (0.22 vs 0.33) over 30 months - and the trial needs 1000 subjects. What absolute rates does that imply?
getAccrualTime.interpretation: The relative intensities scale up to about 23.8 and 35.7 subjects/month so that the total reaches exactly 1000 by month 30. This mirrors how planning actually happens: feasibility teams provide relative ramp-up shapes, the statistician anchors them to the required sample size. The result can feed straight into getSampleSizeSurvival as the accrual specification.

getPiecewiseSurvivalTime.label: Piecewise hazards under a proportional effect
getPiecewiseSurvivalTime.description: The control hazard varies over time - 0.025/month in months 0-6, 0.04 in 6-12, 0.015 after - and treatment reduces it proportionally by 20% (hazard ratio 0.8). What are the treatment-arm hazards?
getPiecewiseSurvivalTime.interpretation: Each treatment hazard is exactly 0.8 x the control hazard (0.020, 0.032, 0.012) - that is what 'proportional hazards' means concretely: the ratio is constant even when the hazards themselves rise and fall. This object is the building block the survival sample size and simulation functions consume; inspect it here once and the piecewise notation elsewhere stops being mysterious.

getLambdaByMedian.label: Median survival to hazard rate
getLambdaByMedian.description: Clinicians quote median survival; the exponential model works in hazard rates. Convert a median of 12 months to its hazard rate.
getLambdaByMedian.interpretation: lambda = log(2) / median = 0.0578 events per subject-month. This one-line conversion is used constantly when translating clinical assumptions into design inputs - and it only holds under the exponential model, which is precisely the assumption worth questioning when survival curves plateau.

getHazardRatioByMedian.label: Medians to hazard ratio
getHazardRatioByMedian.description: Treatment is expected to extend median survival from 12 months (control) to 18 months. What hazard ratio does that correspond to under exponential survival?
getHazardRatioByMedian.interpretation: HR = median2 / median1 = 0.667 - a 50% longer median is the same statement as a one-third lower hazard. Clinical teams reason in medians, design functions want hazard ratios; this converter (and its inverses) is the bridge. It is exact only for exponential survival, a caveat that belongs in every protocol that uses it.

getPiByLambda.label: Hazard rate to event probability
getPiByLambda.description: With a hazard rate of 0.05 events per month, what is the probability a subject has an event within 12 months?
getPiByLambda.interpretation: pi = 1 - exp(-lambda x t) = 0.45: under this hazard, about 45% of subjects have an event within a year. This links the survival world (hazards) to the binary world (event proportions) - useful for sanity-checking hazard assumptions against published event rates, which are usually reported as proportions at a landmark time.

getTestActions.label: What should the committee do at each look?
getTestActions.description: The formal decision rule applied to saved stage results: for each completed stage, stop for efficacy, stop for futility, or continue. Run 'Stage Results' first and save it under the suggested name 'Stage Results' - it appears in the dropdown below.
getTestActions.interpretation: Both completed stages say 'continue': the overall test statistics (1.87, then 2.26) never crossed the efficacy boundaries (3.71, then 2.51). This is the same verdict getAnalysisResults reports, distilled to one word per stage - useful when all a meeting needs is the action, not the full analysis printout.

getConditionalPower.label: Is finishing the trial worth it?
getConditionalPower.description: Given the saved stage results after two of three stages, and 44 subjects still planned for stage 3: what is the chance the trial ends in success? By default the observed effect so far is assumed to continue.
getConditionalPower.interpretation: Conditional power is about 90%: if the effect seen so far is real, the final 44 subjects will very likely push the trial over the line. This is the number a monitoring committee weighs against stopping for futility - and the number adaptive designs use to recalculate sample size. Try nPlanned = 20 to see how a smaller final stage erodes the probability of success.

getConditionalRejectionProbabilities.label: The alpha you carry into the rest of the trial
getConditionalRejectionProbabilities.description: For the saved stage results: the probability, computed under the null hypothesis, of still rejecting at the end given the data observed so far. This is the currency adaptive designs trade in.
getConditionalRejectionProbabilities.interpretation: The conditional rejection probability rises from 0.14 after stage 1 to 0.38 after stage 2 - the accumulating evidence has 'earned' a bigger share of the significance level. If you redesigned the remainder of the trial mid-course, this is exactly the type I error budget the new part would be allowed to spend; that is the CRP principle behind many adaptive methods.

getRepeatedPValues.label: P-values you may quote mid-trial
getRepeatedPValues.description: The p-value companion to repeated confidence intervals: a p-value per stage that stays valid despite the repeated looks, computed from the saved stage results.
getRepeatedPValues.interpretation: The repeated p-value falls from 0.22 after stage 1 to 0.043 after stage 2 - still above the 0.025 significance level, matching the 'continue' decision. Compare 0.043 with the naive p-value for a z of 2.26 (about 0.012): the repeated version is deliberately larger, because it accounts for every look taken and every look still to come.

getFinalPValue.label: The p-value for the final write-up
getFinalPValue.description: The overall p-value of the group sequential trial, adjusted for the sequential design. Uses the saved stage results from two completed stages.
getFinalPValue.interpretation: The result is deliberately empty: with two of three stages done and no boundary crossed, the trial has not stopped, so a final p-value does not exist yet - rpact tells you so rather than inventing one. That refusal is the lesson. Enter data where the boundary is crossed (try stage-2 means of 1.05 vs 0.12 on the Enter data tab) and the final stage and p-value appear.

getFinalConfidenceInterval.label: The confidence interval for the final write-up
getFinalConfidenceInterval.description: The design-adjusted confidence interval and median-unbiased effect estimate reported once a group sequential trial stops. Uses the design and interim dataset from your saved work.
getFinalConfidenceInterval.interpretation: Like the final p-value, the final confidence interval is only defined once the trial stops - here it is empty because stage 2 says 'continue'. When a trial does stop early, the naive interval is biased (trials that stop early tend to overestimate the effect); this function corrects for the sequential stopping. Recreate the dataset with stage-2 means of 1.05 vs 0.12 and rerun: the trial stops at stage 2 with a corrected interval of about [0.30, 1.13].

getWideFormat.label: Your dataset as one row per stage
getWideFormat.description: Shows a saved dataset in wide format: one row per stage, one column per group and quantity, including the cumulative ('overall') values rpact derives from the stage-wise entries.
getWideFormat.interpretation: Check the derived columns: the overall mean for group 1 after stage 2 is 0.575 - the sample-size-weighted average of 0.64 and 0.51. Group sequential analysis always works on these cumulative statistics; seeing them computed from your stage-wise entries makes the analysis output much easier to audit.

getLongFormat.label: Your dataset as one row per stage and group
getLongFormat.description: The same saved dataset in long format: one row per stage-by-group combination - the shape most plotting and modelling tools prefer.
getLongFormat.interpretation: Same numbers, different shape: stage 1 group 1, stage 1 group 2, stage 2 group 1, and so on. If you export interim data to plot recruitment or effects over time in your own scripts, this is the format to start from.

getSimulationCounts.label: Checking the recurrent-events calculation
getSimulationCounts.description: Simulate the recurrent-event trial from the sample size example: 744 subjects accrued over half a year, everyone observed for one year, control rate 0.8 events per year, overdispersion 0.5, tested at rate ratios 0.75 and 1. Benefit is a ratio below 1, hence directionUpper = FALSE.
getSimulationCounts.interpretation: About 82% rejection at rate ratio 0.75 and 3% at 1 - the analytic 80% power and 2.5% type I error recovered by simulation. rpact flags count-data simulation as experimental, which makes this round trip more than a formality: agreement between formula and simulation is how you build trust in a newer method. Try overdispersion = 1 to watch power fall without touching the sample size.

getSimulationMultiArmRates.label: Three arms, binary endpoint, pick the best
getSimulationMultiArmRates.description: The multi-arm selection design with a response-rate endpoint: three active arms against control, best arm at the interim goes on to stage 2. Control response 30%, best arm 50%. Uses the saved 2-stage inverse normal design.
getSimulationMultiArmRates.interpretation: Familywise error 2.9% when no arm beats control (piMax = 0.3), power 47% when the best arm lifts response to 50%. Compare with the multi-arm means example: same structure, notably less power - binary endpoints again. 30 subjects per arm per stage is simply thin for rates; double plannedSubjects and watch the power respond.

getSimulationMultiArmSurvival.label: Three arms, survival endpoint, pick the best
getSimulationMultiArmSurvival.description: Multi-arm selection with a time-to-event endpoint: three active arms, the best continues after the interim. Benefit is a hazard ratio below 1 (best arm 0.7), hence directionUpper = FALSE; the per-stage numbers are cumulative events, not subjects.
getSimulationMultiArmSurvival.interpretation: Familywise error holds at 2.8%; power at hazard ratio 0.7 is only about 37%. That is the honest cost of a multi-arm survival trial: 150 events spread across three comparisons is not many. A two-arm trial detected HR 0.7 with 247 events at 80% power - use that as the anchor when judging how many events a selection design really needs.

getSimulationEnrichmentRates.label: Enrichment with a response-rate endpoint
getSimulationEnrichmentRates.description: The biomarker-enrichment design for rates: subgroup 'S' (40% of patients) responds at 50% versus 30% control; the rest ('R') at 35%. At the interim the trial may restrict to the subpopulation that benefits. Uses the saved 2-stage inverse normal design.

args.effectList: list(subGroups = c("S", "R"), prevalences = c(0.4, 0.6), piControls = c(0.3, 0.3), piTreatments = matrix(c(0.5, 0.35), nrow = 1))

getSimulationEnrichmentRates.interpretation: About 71% probability of rejecting at least one hypothesis. The effectList reads as a table: one row of treatment response rates per subgroup, with control rates and prevalences alongside - the same structure as the enrichment means example, in rate language. The epsilon rule keeps every subpopulation within 0.1 of the best-performing one, a gentler policy than 'best only'.

getSimulationEnrichmentSurvival.label: Enrichment with a survival endpoint
getSimulationEnrichmentSurvival.description: Biomarker enrichment for time-to-event: the treatment works well in subgroup 'S' (hazard ratio 0.6, 40% prevalence) and barely in 'R' (0.9). Benefit is a hazard ratio below 1, hence directionUpper = FALSE; planned numbers are cumulative events.

args.effectList: list(subGroups = c("S", "R"), prevalences = c(0.4, 0.6), hazardRatios = matrix(c(0.6, 0.9), nrow = 1))

getSimulationEnrichmentSurvival.interpretation: About 79% probability of at least one rejection - respectable, because the interim can concentrate stage 2 on subgroup S where the hazard ratio is 0.6. Without enrichment, the full-population effect is a diluted mix of 0.6 and 0.9. This is the oncology-trial workhorse scenario: a biomarker that predicts who benefits, and a design that acts on it mid-trial.

getMedianByLambda.label: Hazard rate to median survival
getMedianByLambda.description: The inverse of the median-to-lambda conversion: a hazard rate of 0.0578 events per subject-month corresponds to what median survival?
getMedianByLambda.interpretation: Median = log(2) / lambda = 12 months - the round trip back from the getLambdaByMedian example. These two converters are used constantly when checking a protocol's assumptions: medians for the clinical sections, hazard rates for the design engine, one line to move between them (exact under exponential survival).

getLambdaByPi.label: Event probability to hazard rate
getLambdaByPi.description: A published trial reports that 30% of control patients had an event within 12 months. What constant hazard rate does that correspond to?
getLambdaByPi.interpretation: lambda = -log(1 - 0.3) / 12 = 0.0297 events per subject-month. This is how literature numbers - usually landmark event proportions - become design inputs. Chain it: feed the result to getMedianByLambda and the same published number reads as a median of about 23 months.

getPiByMedian.label: Median survival to event probability
getPiByMedian.description: If median survival is 12 months, what fraction of subjects have an event within 12 months?
getPiByMedian.interpretation: Exactly 0.5 - by definition of the median, and a reassuring sanity check that the exponential machinery is self-consistent. Change eventTime to 24 and the answer becomes 0.75: under a constant hazard, three quarters have an event within two medians.

getMedianByPi.label: Event probability to median survival
getMedianByPi.description: 45% of control subjects are expected to have an event within 12 months. What median survival does that imply?
getMedianByPi.interpretation: About 13.9 months. Landmark proportions and medians are two dialects for the same survival assumption; this converter (with getPiByMedian as its inverse) translates between them so you can cross-check a protocol's stated median against the event rates it also quotes.

getHazardRatioByLambda.label: Two hazard rates to a hazard ratio
getHazardRatioByLambda.description: Treatment arm hazard 0.04 events per subject-month, control 0.0578. What is the hazard ratio?
getHazardRatioByLambda.interpretation: HR = 0.04 / 0.0578 = 0.69 - just a division, but having it as a function keeps conversion chains readable in the R code panel. Note the convention used everywhere in rpact: group 1 is treatment, group 2 is control, and a ratio below 1 favors treatment.

getHazardRatioByPi.label: Two event probabilities to a hazard ratio
getHazardRatioByPi.description: At 12 months, 30% of treatment and 40% of control subjects are expected to have an event. What hazard ratio is that?
getHazardRatioByPi.interpretation: HR = log(1 - 0.3) / log(1 - 0.4) = 0.70. This is the converter to reach for when a publication only reports landmark event rates: two proportions in, a design-ready hazard ratio out - under the exponential assumption, which is worth stating in the protocol.

getPi1ByPi2AndHazardRatio.label: Implied treatment event rate
getPi1ByPi2AndHazardRatio.description: Control has a 45% event probability at 12 months and the target hazard ratio is 0.7. What event probability in the treatment arm does that combination imply?
getPi1ByPi2AndHazardRatio.interpretation: About 34% - the hazard ratio of 0.7 translates into an 11-point drop in the 12-month event rate here. This is a great communication tool: clinicians often find '45% down to 34% at one year' far more meaningful than 'hazard ratio 0.7', and this function makes the two statements provably the same.

getPi2ByPi1AndHazardRatio.label: Implied control event rate
getPi2ByPi1AndHazardRatio.description: Working backwards: the treatment arm is expected to have a 35% event probability at 12 months under a hazard ratio of 0.7. What control event rate is being assumed?
getPi2ByPi1AndHazardRatio.interpretation: About 46%. Use this direction when reverse-engineering someone else's design: given their treatment-arm assumption and hazard ratio, you recover the control-arm rate they must have believed - and can check it against historical data.

getLambda1ByLambda2AndHazardRatio.label: Implied treatment hazard rate
getLambda1ByLambda2AndHazardRatio.description: Control hazard 0.0578 per subject-month, target hazard ratio 0.7: what treatment hazard is being assumed?
getLambda1ByLambda2AndHazardRatio.interpretation: 0.0405 per subject-month - simply 0.7 x 0.0578, the definition of proportional hazards in one multiplication. Feed it to getMedianByLambda to state the same assumption as a median of about 17 months, ready for the protocol synopsis.

getLambda2ByLambda1AndHazardRatio.label: Implied control hazard rate
getLambda2ByLambda1AndHazardRatio.description: The treatment arm is assumed to have hazard 0.04 per subject-month under a hazard ratio of 0.7. What control hazard does that imply?
getLambda2ByLambda1AndHazardRatio.interpretation: 0.0571 per subject-month (0.04 / 0.7). Together with its three siblings this closes the loop: any two of {lambda1, lambda2, hazard ratio} determine the third, and there is a converter for every direction you might need to travel.

getPiecewiseExponentialDistribution.label: Event probabilities under a piecewise hazard
getPiecewiseExponentialDistribution.description: For the piecewise control hazard used in the survival planning examples (0.025/month in months 0-6, 0.04 in 6-12, 0.015 after), what is the probability of an event by months 6, 12, 18, and 24?
getPiecewiseExponentialDistribution.interpretation: 14% by month 6, 32% by month 12, then only 38% and 43% - the curve nearly flattens once the hazard drops to 0.015. This is the calculation to run before believing a piecewise assumption: seeing the implied event curve, month by month, is the fastest way to spot an assumption that contradicts the historical data.

getPiecewiseExponentialQuantile.label: Median survival under a piecewise hazard
getPiecewiseExponentialQuantile.description: Same piecewise hazard: at what time has half the population had an event? (quantile = 0.5 asks for the median.)
getPiecewiseExponentialQuantile.interpretation: About 32 months - far beyond the 12-month window where the hazard was high, because the low late hazard (0.015) stretches the upper half of the distribution enormously. A single 'median survival' number hides this shape; the piecewise machinery is how you keep the shape in the design.

getPiecewiseExponentialRandomNumbers.label: Simulated event times from a piecewise hazard
getPiecewiseExponentialRandomNumbers.description: Draw 10 random event times from the same piecewise hazard - the building block Monte Carlo survival simulations are made of.
getPiecewiseExponentialRandomNumbers.interpretation: Ten event times, different on every run (this generator has no seed argument - true randomness is the point here). Look at the spread: a few early events from the high-hazard year, and a long tail stretching past month 50, exactly the shape the distribution function predicted. This is what getSimulationSurvival does internally, hundreds of thousands of times.
